title: A Hormone Chain, Held in Check

scenes.tts: A physician castrated young roosters. Then he put a testis back into the belly of some of them, cut off from its original nerves. Those birds still grew combs and behaved like roosters. How can an organ change the whole body without its own nerves? In this bird, the testis acted through something carried in the blood.
scenes.visual: A testis block moves into the cockerel outline, the link to the original nerves is crossed out, a comb block lights up, a blood bar carries yellow dots between them.
scenes.narration: A physician castrated young roosters. Then he put a testis back into the belly of some of them, cut off from its original nerves. Those birds still grew combs and behaved like roosters. How can an organ change the whole body without its own nerves? In this bird, the testis acted through something carried in the blood.

scenes.tts: A hormone is a chemical that one group of cells releases into the blood. The blood carries it to distant target cells. Those cells have receptors for it. A receptor is a protein that binds the hormone and changes what the cell does. Think of a radio broadcast. It reaches every house, and only houses with a tuned set hear it.
scenes.visual: Gland releases yellow dots into a blood bar; three cells below, two with receptor cups respond and turn green, one without stays grey.

scenes.tts: In mammals, the hypothalamus sits at the base of the brain. It controls the pituitary gland. Take the stress axis in humans. The hypothalamus releases C R H, and C R H makes the anterior pituitary release A C T H. Then A C T H makes the adrenal cortex produce cortisol.
scenes.caption: In mammals, the hypothalamus sits at the base of the brain. It controls the pituitary gland. Take the stress axis in humans. The hypothalamus releases CRH, and CRH makes the anterior pituitary release ACTH. Then ACTH makes the adrenal cortex produce cortisol.
scenes.visual: Three gland blocks light up in order with arrows labelled CRH and ACTH, then a cortisol chip drops from the adrenal cortex.
scenes.narration: In mammals, the hypothalamus sits at the base of the brain. It controls the pituitary gland. Take the stress axis in humans. The hypothalamus releases CRH, and CRH makes the anterior pituitary release ACTH. Then ACTH makes the adrenal cortex produce cortisol.

scenes.tts: Now the loop closes. In humans, rising cortisol lowers C R H and A C T H. That is negative feedback, a response that opposes the change that caused it. So a rise in cortisol reduces the drive that produced it. Feedback acts at both the hypothalamus and the pituitary.

scenes.visual: Red inhibition lines run from the cortisol chip back to the hypothalamus and the pituitary; the CRH and ACTH arrows dim.

scenes.tts: Feedback does not hold a hormone at one fixed value. In humans, cortisol rises and falls over the day. It also comes in pulses roughly every sixty to ninety minutes. In a study of fifteen healthy men, whose own cortisol was blocked, the same daily dose on different schedules changed how their brains responded to emotional stimuli. In this one small study, the timing itself carried information.

scenes.tts: Other animals run the same logic on different molecules, so name the animal each time. In the bug Rod nee us prolix us, a moult-promoting signal travels in the blood and is needed for the moult. In frog tadpoles, thyroid hormone drives metamorphosis. To read any loop, remove or add one hormone, then predict the rest of its loop.
